US President Donald Trump has renewed his controversial “51st state” jibe at Canada as tensions between the two North American neighbours escalate over a fresh tariff dispute.
Trump took to Truth Social to criticise Canada after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa would respond to Washington’s latest tariffs with a “dollar for dollar” measure.
“Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” Trump wrote.
Trump’s ‘51st state’ remark
Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st US state. He first began making the remarks publicly in 2025, when Justin Trudeau was Canada’s prime minister, amid growing tensions over trade and tariffs.
The US president has continued to use the idea while arguing that Canada benefits economically from its relationship with the United States without meeting Washington’s demands on trade.
The latest comments come after trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa failed to produce an agreement.
US-Canada tariff row escalates
The United States has announced a 50% tariff on Canadian imports after the latest trade negotiations fell through.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada had declined to finalise a trade agreement under terms that Washington claimed had been agreed earlier in the week.
According to Greer, the US had offered to reduce tariffs on certain sectors, including steel and aluminium, but Canada did not accept the proposed terms.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, however, described the US move as an “attack on Canada” and said Ottawa would protect the country’s economy and national interests.
Carney also said Canada would introduce a “dollar for dollar” response to match the US tariffs. Details of the countermeasures are expected to be announced later this week.
Carney criticises US trade approach
Carney has pushed back against Washington’s position, arguing that last-minute changes made by the US were unfair and undermined confidence in any potential trade agreement.
He described the changes as “unfair” and “uneconomic”, while questioning the reliability of future deals with Washington.
The latest dispute adds another layer of tension to the relationship between the two countries, which share one of the world’s largest bilateral trading relationships.
Trump had previously said that Washington should be able to reach a deal with Canada, pointing to his relationship with Carney. However, the collapse of the latest negotiations and the subsequent tariff announcement have once again brought trade tensions to the forefront.

U.S.-Israeli War in Iran
— Iran accused the United States of violating the sovereignty of other countries through sweeping new sanctions due to be announced on Monday. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the threat to punish Iran’s trading partners an “abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism,” while Mr. Trump warned of “tremendous economic consequences” for any country whose financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities provide Tehran with an economic lifeline. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has promised the “toughest sanctions in history,” aimed particularly at China, which buys more than 80% of Iran’s shipped oil.

Participating operators register their voyages with U.S. Central Command, frequently switch off their transponders, and can call upon American warships, aircraft, and helicopters to intercept Iranian missiles and drones. Tankers using the corridor carried ca. 5 million barrels daily in July, compared with the 15 million that passed through the strait before the war. The protection has not eliminated the danger: At least 15 ships using the southern route have been struck since June, killing two mariners and wounding 16.
— Mr. Trump threatened to unleash what he termed an “economic D-Day” against Iran and countries that continue to trade with it, although details were scant. The campaign is expected to target Iranian oil sales, financial transactions, and sanctions-evasion networks in an effort to force Tehran to abandon its nuclear program and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. It would also impose severe secondary sanctions and economic penalties on any country, business, or financial institution that continues to trade with or support Iran as the war approaches the six-month mark.
— The USS George Washington arrived in the Middle East to relieve the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln, which has spent more than 250 days deployed and more than 200 days without a port call. Families of sailors aboard the Lincoln have reported food shortages, plumbing failures, exhaustion, and deteriorating morale. The Navy has not said when the carrier will return to the United States.
— Somali piracy has surged in the western Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden. Pirates hijacked two vessels in four days as naval forces in the region remained strained by the Iran war and Houthi attacks. The Cameroon-flagged Lutuf, carrying Turkish military equipment, was seized with its ten-member crew off Puntland. On Thursday, six armed Somali pirates hijacked the sanctioned product tanker Sibu 1, a vessel linked to Iran’s “shadow fleet,” in the Gulf of Aden and diverted it towards Somalia. Also hijacked in recent weeks were the tanker Asana and Honour 25.

Russo-Ukrainian War
— Mr. Putin threatened to retaliate against Ukraine’s “most sensitive economic sectors,” accusing Kyiv of opening a “Pandora’s box” by escalating attacks on Russian economic infrastructure. The warning followed weeks of Ukrainian strikes against facilities operated by Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, which Kyiv says support Russian military logistics, and the first strike against a warehouse belonging to its smaller rival Ozon. Mr. Putin pointed to attacks on Ukraine’s ports and grain-export infrastructure as the type of retaliation Moscow would intensify.
— Ukraine launched a wave of attacks against strategic targets in Russia and Russian-occupied Ukraine, including an Ozon fulfillment center in Chapayevsk and the nearby Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region, more than 620 miles (1,000 km) from the front. Ozon, Russia’s second-largest online marketplace, halted operations at the warehouse after workers were wounded, while Ukraine’s military said that the refinery was set ablaze. At least 10 people were killed across Russia and Russian-occupied Ukraine; Moscow said that its forces shot down 457 drones overnight.
— Russia deliberately targeted critical infrastructure during a massive overnight missile and drone attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region, the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said. At least 17 people were killed and more than 40 injured, while homes, a school, a children’s medical center, and industrial facilities were damaged. The strikes also disrupted hot-water service in parts of the capital.
— Russian attacks on major food warehouses have left temporary gaps on supermarket shelves in Kyiv, an unfamiliar sight after more than four years of war. Fresh produce, meat, dairy products, eggs, and some grains have been affected, but retailers are rerouting deliveries and officials said there was no general food shortage.

The measures took effect after negotiations collapsed on Friday despite Mr. Trump’s three-day delay intended to allow talks to continue.

Gunmen killed more than 40 people and abducted over 100 others in coördinated attacks on several villages in western Nigeria. The assailants reportedly rounded up residents and forced them into nearby forests. Police said that the attackers were probably members of criminal gangs that abduct villagers for ransom. Such gangs have stepped up attacks in the remote region in recent months, taking advantage of sparse security coverage and extensive forest hideouts.

The Luxury Collection, a unit of Marriott International and formerly a Starwood brand, launched The Luxury Collection Expeditions, a new immersive travel program. The offering comprises three categories: Private Tailored Journeys, Day Discoveries, and Residencies and Collaborations. Private Tailored Journeys are bespoke, multiday cultural tours; possibilities include the Imperial Journey to Japan, which unfolds over ten days across Tokyo, Kyoto, and Nara, and the Grand Italia Rally, which takes inspiration from Italy’s endurance road races and puts guests behind the wheel of a classic Italian automobile on a route from Milan to Venice and Florence. Day Discoveries are local one-day excursions that focus on a culinary tradition, a cultural practice, or an area of great natural beauty and can range from winemaking to marine science. Finally, Residencies and Collaborations are limited-time opportunities to learn from leading scientists or master craftsmen in a particular field.

Marriott’s Luxury Collection of hotels, a portfolio that dates back over a century to 1906 and the founding of the Compagnia Italiana Grandi Alberghi, or Italian Grand Hotel Company, is a global group of hotels and resorts that encompasses some of the world’s most historic and storied properties. At the time of its founding, CIGA owned some of the finest hotels in Italy and later expanded to Austria, Sardinia, and Spain. The Luxury Collection brand traces its name back to 1992, when ITT Sheraton (Sheraton, which was founded in 1937, was taken over by ITT in 1968) applied the name to 28 of its best hotels and 33 of its Sheraton Towers hotel-within-a-hotel properties. Its flagship was the St. Regis in New York City, a hotel that eventually begat its own brand. The group received a tremendous boost in 1994 when ITT Sheraton acquired CIGA, keeping CIGA’s four horses of St. Mark logo. The majority of CIGA’s hotels became part of what was by then known as the ITT Sheraton Luxury Collection. The Luxury Collection was expanded once again when Starwood acquired ITT Sheraton in 1998 and again in 2016 when Marriott acquired Starwood.

New York City expanded its efforts to adapt to increasingly severe rainstorms along two markedly different tracks: retreating from some of the most flood-prone blocks in Queens and restoring a Bronx stream buried in the sewer system more than a century ago. Through its Resilient Acquisitions program, the city is gauging whether homeowners in Hollis, a neighborhood in Queens which sits atop a former pond, and the Kissena Park section of Flushing, where a swamp and creek once stood, would voluntarily sell their properties. The outreach expands beyond the Jewel Streets on the Queens-Brooklyn border, an area known as the Hole because it lies below sea level and lacks a connection to the city sewer system; acquired land could become parkland, natural areas, or stormwater-storage facilities. In the Bronx, meanwhile, a $149.5 million project scheduled to begin this fall will “daylight” Tibbetts Brook, returning part of the stream buried in 1912 to an open channel running from Van Cortlandt Park towards the Harlem River. The brook now pours four million to five million gallons (15 million to 19 million l) of clean water into the sewer system each day, contributing to flooding and untreated sewage overflows during heavy rain. Restoring it should divert ca. 220 million gallons (833 million l) annually, create new green space, and test whether New York can once again use its natural waterways as infrastructure.

South Korea sent the PanStar Acro, a container ship operated by PanStar, from Busan New Port on Saturday on the country’s first commercial voyage to Europe through the Arctic. Carrying 837 twenty-foot equivalent units of automobile parts, chemicals, and other cargo, the vessel will enter the Northern Sea Route through the Bering Strait and follow Russia’s Arctic coast before calling at Felixstowe, Rotterdam, and Gdansk; the round trip is expected to take 40 to 45 days. The passage is ca. 4,300 miles (7,000 km) shorter and ten days faster than the conventional route through the Suez Canal, giving the experiment new urgency as the U.S.-Israeli War in Iran disrupts shipping through the Middle East. Seoul hopes to make Busan a global shipping hub and establish the route as a regular trade corridor by 2030, but the voyage requires coöperation with Russia, potentially complicating relations with Western allies, while environmental groups warn that emissions from increased shipping could accelerate the melting of the sea ice that made the route navigable in the first place.
____________________________________
After years of trying to steer customers towards its proprietary payment systems, Walmart said it would begin accepting Apple Pay, Google Pay, Samsung Pay, and contactless credit and debit cards at selected Walmart and Sam’s Club locations effective on 24 August. The retailer expects to introduce tap-to-pay at every U.S. store and club by the end of 2026 and at its fuel stations by mid-2027. Walmart had resisted standard near-field communication payments in favor of its QR-code-based Walmart Pay system and Sam’s Club’s Scan & Go; it had also participated in CurrentC, an unsuccessful retailer-backed attempt to supplant Apple Pay that shut down in 2016. Apple Pay debuted in 2014 and is now accepted at more than 85% of U.S. retailers, leaving Walmart one of the last major holdouts, although its Canadian stores began accepting it in 2020. Walmart Pay and Scan & Go will remain available alongside the new options.
____________________________________
Applied Atomics, a nuclear-energy startup founded by former SpaceX engineers Ben Kellie and Paul Keutelian, secured an exclusive land-based license to revive mPower, a small modular reactor developed by BWX Technologies. The original project consumed ca. $400 million before BWXT shelved it in 2017 as inexpensive natural gas, the reaction to the Fukushima disaster, and weak demand from utilities destroyed its commercial prospects. At its heart is a 120′ (36.6 m) electrically powered mock reactor outside Lynchburg, Virginia, built to replicate the operation of a nuclear plant without using radioactive material and left dormant for nearly a decade. The proposed factory-built reactor would use conventional pressurized light-water technology and standard low-enriched uranium to generate 195 megawatts of electricity, enough to power ca. 155,000 homes; several units could instead be grouped beside a large data center or industrial complex. Applied Atomics says that the surviving engineering work, regulatory filings, and test facility could eliminate years of development and allow its first commercial reactor to begin operating in about five years. The bet remains far from proven: the company must restart the federal certification process, raise billions of dollars, address safety and waste concerns, and overcome an American small-reactor industry that has yet to place a single commercial unit into service.
____________________________________
New York City’s vaunted 911 emergency-dispatch system failed for ca. seven hours on Tuesday, preventing as many as 400 people from reaching an operator. From 3:13 a.m. to 10:19 a.m. (03.13 to 10.19) local time, nearly 1,700 of the 5,659 calls routed through Public Safety Answering Center II in the Bronx were affected, with callers and operators unable to hear one another. The larger figure includes duplicate calls and automated alarms; city officials estimate that as many as 400 individual callers failed to connect. The city’s other emergency center in Brooklyn continued operating normally. PSAC II was completed in 2016 as a backup to the Brooklyn center following a troubled modernization program begun in 2004 that ultimately cost more than $2 billion. Officials had not determined the cause, although sources said that a technology change scheduled for 3 a.m. may have blocked the calls and that the backup system failed to operate as intended. The city said that the breakdown was not a cyberattack, but it remained unclear whether anyone had been denied urgently needed police, fire, or medical assistance.
____________________________________
The first emergency telephone number deployed anywhere in the world was “999” in London on July 1, 1937. It soon spread throughout the rest of the country. “116” was adopted as an emergency number in Los Angeles, California in 1946. “911” was first used in the U.S. in 1968 and became a standard in the 1980s. “112,” first introduced in larger cities in West Germany for the fire department after “110” had been deployed for calls to the police, became a European Union standard for emergency calls in 1991. As a result, the three most widely recognized emergency numbers are 112, 911, and 999.
____________________________________

Tesla said that it will recall 2.98 million imported and China-built electric vehicles in China beginning on 25 September after regulators found that Tesla’s mechanical emergency door releases could be difficult to locate or operate following a severe collision that disables the electrical system. The action encompasses Model 3, Model Y, Model S, and Model X automobiles and is Tesla’s largest recall in China. The automaker will install warning labels identifying the emergency releases and issue an over-the-air software update that automatically lowers the windows after a collision, making it easier for occupants to escape or rescuers to gain access. Tesla is one of nine automakers recalling a record 4.3 million vehicles in China over similar concerns. Flush-mounted electronic door handles, a design popularized by Tesla, have drawn increasing scrutiny following accidents in which occupants became trapped inside burning automobiles. China, which has adopted an increasingly strict approach to electric-vehicle safety, will prohibit concealed door handles on new automobiles beginning in 2027. U.S. regulators are considering new safety standards addressing the same danger, but no comparable American recall has been announced.
____________________________________
Nederlandse Spoorwegen, the Netherlands’ largest railway operator, adopted a new house rule barring passengers from using train seats for their luggage beginning on 4 September. Travelers must instead keep their bags on their laps, beneath their seats, or in luggage racks. Previously, luggage had to be removed only when another passenger asked to occupy the seat. “We aim to ensure that passengers no longer have to ask each other to remove a bag from a seat,” an NS spokesman said. The new rule states that “seats are for passengers” and that hand luggage must not unnecessarily occupy one. NS said the measure is intended to establish a clear social norm and prevent disputes, not to punish passengers; conductors will issue reminders, but no fines are planned.
____________________________________
The New York metropolitan area surpassed the San Francisco Bay Area as North America’s largest technology-talent market by headcount for the first time, according to CBRE Group’s 2026 Scoring Tech Talent report. New York’s technology workforce reached 394,300 in 2025, an increase of 30,640 over three years, while the Bay Area’s fell by 23,900 to 375,730 amidst widespread layoffs of workers in non-AI positions. CBRE, an American commercial real estate services and investment firm, attributed New York’s growth in part to hiring by financial-services companies and the rapid expansion of AI-related employment. The company defines “tech talent” as workers in more than 20 technology-oriented occupations across all industries, meaning that a software developer employed by a bank counts alongside one working for a technology company. San Francisco nevertheless retained first place in CBRE’s broader ranking, which weighs 13 factors including workforce concentration, research-and-development investment, and the supply of new talent; New York ranked fourth. sources.news_title: A trade war with the U.S. may not be great, but the day after Labour Day 2026 is a great moment for it to start
sources.text:
If a country had to pick a moment to strike back with targeted countervailing tariffs at the Trump Administration’s habitual bad-faith trade bargaining, surely it would be difficult to imagine a better moment than the day after Labour Day 2026.
As is now well understood by almost everybody on both sides of the world’s longest undefended border, tariffs are going to hit us all regardless of whether we live in the United States or Canada.
But unlike the president of the United States, Canada’s head of government isn’t facing a crucial mid-term election only two months later. That’s long enough for Canadian counter-tariffs that really bite to noticed south of the Medicine Line, but gives the American administration a couple of weeks to think about the implications of that.
One would think it would be a powerful incentive for Donald Trump to TACO and send his negotiators back to the table without the last-minute attack on Canadian sovereignty that killed the deal Friday night.
A little earlier and the likely American counter-counter response might have hurt too much. A little later and it might have been too late for American voters to notice before the mid-terms. To paraphrase Dr. Johnson, it remains to be seen if this is enough to concentrate Mr. Trump’s mind, what’s left of it, wonderfully.
This probably explains why Canadian provincial and federal leaders of all political stripes immediately closed ranks behind Prime Minister Mark Carney, the leader who had the awful responsibility of deciding whether or not to pull the plug on “negotiations” with a government that was neither capable of making an agreement nor sticking to it.
Why, even federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre appears to be on side, vowing in a social media statement Saturday that “Conservatives will always put our country first.” He added, “Conservatives support action to protect Canadians and our industries targeted by these unfair U.S. tariffs.”
There was only one exception. It was Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, of course.
Ms. Smith piously insisted tariffs are always a terrible thing and Canada should immediately roll over and let the United States have its way with us.
On her Saturday morning bi-monthly radio program, Alberta’s United Conservative Party premier reluctantly agreed that Mr. Carney was right to withdraw from bargaining.
But she indicated she wanted no part of taking effective countermeasures – especially if Canada’s richest province has to do its part and feel some of the pain along with everyone else.
“I know, emotionally, it feels good to retaliate, I get that, but let’s remember what happens when we retaliate,” she complained to a softball question pitched by the radio program’s tame host.
A statement on social media late Friday evening came closer to what she likely really thinks: “Alberta will continue to advocate for a strong tariff free relationship between Canada and the U.S.,” she said. “I will be urging the federal government to restart negotiations as soon as possible.”
So while Ontario’s Conservative Premier, Doug Ford, said “Ontario is ready to do its part,” his Alberta Conservative counterpart tacitly indicated, forget about it.
Rob Anderson, Ms. Smith’s chief of staff and some would say the province’s de facto premier, tweeted similar sentiments just after midnight Saturday morning. “Don’t give in to knee-jerk actions that feel good in the moment but only hurt ourselves,” he whinged. “We need to be smarter not more tough guy-er.”
Mr. Anderson, of course, is one of the authors of the Free Alberta Strategy that is driving Ms. Smith’s separation referendum in October, and I’m sure he worries that an excess of Canadian patriotism in response to Mr. Trump’s trade depredations may set back the Alberta separation/U.S. assimilation project which has been successfully flying largely under the public radar.
Interestingly, back on Aug. 15, a week before the negotiations between Canada and the U.S. fell apart, a story in The Globe and Mail included an interesting hint about how the Trump Administration views the Smith Government’s pressure on Ottawa to permit pipelines to be built of every point of the compass.
“The U.S. is demanding a right of first refusal on Canadian critical minerals; that Canada complete its purchase of U.S. F-35 fighter jets; that Ottawa buy U.S. tech such as radar planes as part of joining Mr. Trump’s planned Golden Dome missile defence system; and that Washington receive some guarantee on future supplies of oil and gas,” the story said, citing both Canadian and U.S. sources.
This suggests, one would think, that the Trump government – which clearly would like to end all Canadian trade with China, and possibly Europe as well – would not look with favour on a Canadian pipeline to B.C.’s North Coast to ship Alberta heavy crude to Asia (read China).
How would Ms. Smith feel about that? Probably not as bad as you might imagine, dear readers, since her devotion to Mr. Trump and his MAGA ideology is well known, her separation machinations appear to be motivated as much by a wish for U.S. assimilation as actual independence, and her abiding hatred of the things like public health care that make Canada a better country to live in than the United States.
It’s interesting to note that in light of Mr. Poilievre’s complaint in early August that Mr. Carney was giving away too much to the Americans, U.S. Vice-President JD Vance has made it obvious the Trump Administration would prefer Ontario Conservative MP Jamil Jivani as leader of Canada’s federal Opposition party.
Mr. Vance and his college pal Mr. Jivani, it must be noted, seem like a real pair of weirdos, probably not fully trusted by either of their bosses.
Be that as it may, calling “this guy Pierre Poilievre, who is the leader of the Conservatives in Canada” a “non-entity” at a, Aug. 9 fund-raiser in Southampton, New York, Mr. Vance lauded Mr. Jivani, “this, like, random MP who has a good relationship with us” for his behind-the-scenes advocacy. It’s pretty obvious where Mr. Vance got his impression of Mr. Poilievre.
Despite the Canadian Press reporter who received a recording of the event stating that Mr. Vance meant Mr. Jivani’s advocacy for Canada, this is not actually clear from the context provided in the story.
Mr. Poilievre’s response to his MP’s apparent effort to undermine his leadership was lame, telling CP he’s asked all his MPs with contacts in the U.S. to “fight for tariff-free trade.” He’ll have to do better than with undeclared rivals that if he wants to keep his job.
Danielle Smith would love to do whatever Donald Trump wants. She doesn’t care about Canada. Furthermore, Danielle Smith is good at flapping her gums. What did her meeting in Florida with Donald Trump accomplish?Nothing. Kevin O’Leary was there, and Danielle Smith was likely trying to get an AI data centre for Alberta.
The risk for Trump is his trade war with Canada, which seemed to be close to cooling down but is now heating up again, starts to be seen by his country like his ill advised Middle East conflict. Unnecessary, unending and harmful for their own interests. They seem to have figured out tarrifs are a actually a tax on them and their leader in his second term is an unrestrained bull in a china shop causing damage.
In Canada a familiar pattern is happening with most Premiers and leaders backing the PM, with Smith’s support being the most tepid and the Federal opposition leader’s being the least relevant. Vance’s comments again are not very helpful for the CPC or its leader.
However the CPC leader at least seems to trying to appear to be loyal to Canada. If this conflict continues, it will be interesting if due to her ambivalence, the impression of Smith as a traitor takes more hold.
In spite of what she says, it is very clear to any Albertans that cut through the BS what Smith really has in mind, and it certainly is not what is good for Albertans, just what might be good for her. It is a real embarrassment to see her off in the far forty and nowhere in line with the other Premiers.
Smith is playing a dangerous game with the rest of the country. Speaking from Ontario, one of the hardest hit provinces by the tariffs, it’s being noticed that Alberta (and Saskatchewan) are not willing to make sacrifices for the country. You can hear it in (fairly low key) complaints from Doug Ford. If things get really bad and central Canada suffers for a prolonged period of time while Alberta prospers, I fear that the imagined hostility that many Albertans perceive emanating from upper and lower Canada will become actual hostility.
At least Alberta separatists and conservatives will have something real to complain about.
Trust Smith to be the only Premier to support the Trump administration. She most likely has MAGA embordered on her knickers. She is so hell-bent on breaking Canada up, it’s really quite frightening, but I do think that her base is starting to realize she losing public support and they’ll start discussing her demise. I also think, that even the staunchest UPC supporter, supports what Carney has done and is questioning Smiths position. It’ll be very interesting to see the outcome of the Calgary by-election.
Marlaina has shown us repeatedly that she could not care less about Canada. She is a treasonous snake who only cares about herself. Why do Albertans put up with it?
We must admit that Carney’s negotiation strategy was excellent: negotiate to the last minute, maintaining the suspense, and then pull out intirely.
This is the political equivalent of what Iran did in West Asia and it is a complete victory: no fights among provinces on this or that concession, a united front (minus Alberta) against the bullies Vance and Trump, a big stature boost to Canada (and to Carney himself).
Now let’s face the music!
Perhaps the RCMP’s review of possible treasonous activity by Smith is not so far fetched after all. However, the real target of an investigation should be Rath & Slyvestre.
Has Premier Smith been promised a plum position as unelected prime minister in the post-separation-Alberta-referendum-on-a-referendum-apocalypse-US-territory-of-Canada, with absolutely zero foreign interference which she has already acknowledged? Maybe a hefty salary to go along with it and a palace fit for the Princess of Petroleum? (Not a cottage, people, are you joking?) Let it be adorned with 24 karats of cats!
Who better to crush us under the heel of her rhinestone cowboy boot than the woman in the 10-gallon wool felt hat who is so unemotional that she is entirely incapable of crying an actual tear, although God knows she tried to squeeze one out once. (How do you normal people with human feelings do it? It’s painful, so impossibly painful.)
Finally, she is getting closer to world dominance, or at least dominance over a dominion and a title worthy of her high intellect and charm. Don’t forget the charm. Bend the knee or Mommy Dearest will order spankings for all of you whiny, emotional Alberto-soon-to-be-ex-Canadians and all the rest of you about-to-be-ex-Canadians who haven’t realized it yet and don’t get to vote. Watch out if she gives Bruce McAllister that throat slashing signal. Cut the mic, you’re all going down! Proceed directly to Bruce for your punishment, or if he’s busy Rob Anderson, or perhaps tough guy Jamil Jivani but definitely not Pierre Poilievre, the “non-entity”. If you’re very obedient, get in the other line for your fascist pancakes. Don’t know what those are? They’re usually served cold and half-raw in the middle, proving that people will line up for anything, no matter how bad it is and how bad it is for them. Like now. Buckle up, cowpokes. This ride is going to be a “100”.
Maitres chez nous.

sources.news_title: US Canada Trade War: Mark Carney Retaliates Against Trump With New Tariffs
sources.text:
The diplomatic and economic relationship between the United States and Canada has taken a sharp turn for the worse as a long-standing trade dispute has transformed into an open tariff war, while tensions reached a breaking point after the final round of negotiations regarding trade agreements ended without a resolution. In a significant escalation, the Trump administration moved to implement a 50 percent tariff on Canadian goods valued at approximately 20 billion dollars. This aggressive move prompted an immediate and firm response from Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who declared that Canada would respond to the American tariffs with a dollar-for-dollar retaliatory strategy.
Canada Announces Retaliatory Measures
On Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney officially announced Canada's plan for retaliatory action against the United States. During his address, he specified that starting from September 8, Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs on goods arriving from the United States. Carney emphasized the gravity of the situation, stating that when a country is attacked, it finds itself in a state of war, and he characterized the recent American economic measures as a direct attack on Canada. The decision to retaliate follows the imposition of the 50 percent tariff by the Trump administration, which is estimated to impact nearly 5 percent of Canada's annual exports to its southern neighbor.
Impacted Industries and Products
The tariffs imposed by the United States target a variety of Canadian exports, including hockey sticks, small wooden implements used in medical equipment, and several other industrial products. In response, Carney outlined the sectors that will be hit by Canada's retaliatory tariffs. These include American dairy products, steel, household appliances, agricultural machinery, electronic goods, and products related to pulp and paper. This comprehensive list indicates that the Canadian government is prepared to strike back across multiple sectors of the American economy to match the scale of the initial US tariffs.
Carney Addresses the Nation
In a detailed 22 minute speech, Prime Minister Carney explained the rationale behind the breakdown in negotiations. He revealed that Canada was initially prepared to make significant concessions to reach a deal. Ottawa had offered to remove existing retaliatory tariffs on American aluminum, steel, and motor vehicles if Washington agreed to substantially reduce its own tariffs. On top of that, the Canadian government was willing to encourage provinces to resume the sale of American liquor. However, Carney noted that the final terms proposed by the Trump administration were fundamentally unacceptable. He remarked that the US side demanded too much while offering too little in return, and Canada wasn't willing to compromise its national sovereignty or weaken its key industries to satisfy those demands.
The Breakdown of Negotiations
The collapse of the trade talks is particularly striking because, only 48 hours prior, there were strong hopes for a successful agreement. For three days, Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and American negotiator Jamieson Greer had been engaged in intensive discussions in Washington. Officials from both sides appeared to be nearing a consensus. However, in the final stages of the talks, the United States introduced new conditions that Canada found impossible to accept. These conditions reportedly sought to limit Canada's ability to enter into trade agreements with other nations. Consequently, Canada halted the negotiations and recalled its delegation to Ottawa.
A Fundamental Shift in Relations
Prime Minister Carney observed that this trade war has brought about a fundamental shift in the relationship between Canada and the United States. He stated that Canada has recognized from the beginning that the United States has changed, famously remarking that sometimes the American signature is written in pencil, implying a lack of permanence or reliability in their commitments. Carney made it clear that Canada isn't looking to return to the old status quo of the relationship. This sentiment was echoed by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who expressed full support for the dollar-for-dollar retaliatory action, stating that every option must be considered to protect Canadian interests.
The American Perspective
On the other side, the American administration has placed the blame for the failed talks squarely on Canada, while trump administration officials claimed they had offered concessions in key sectors such as timber, steel, and automobiles. American trade negotiator Jamieson Greer asserted that Washington had provided an opportunity for Canada to secure a better deal than what was previously on the table, but suggested that the Canadian side was unwilling to accept it. Despite these claims, Canada remains firm in its position, highlighting that it has successfully secured 20 new agreements and economic partnerships over the past year, doubling its potential market access and proving its status as a preferred global partner for many other nations.

Carney said US demands revealed the limits of their commitment to a true economic partnership and he had directed the country's negotiators to return to Ottawa.

Carney said on Saturday that the US asked too much and offered too little.
He said Ottawa felt that the two countries were moving towards a mutually beneficial agreement but in recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were 'uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada'.
He said it raised questions on reliability of any deal. 'They asked too much, and they offered too little,' he said.
Carney said the US stance revealed the limits of their commitment to a true economic partnership. 'Last evening, I suspended trade negotiations with the United States and directed our negotiators to return to Ottawa,' he added.
The development came after trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down late Friday night, with the United States imposing a 50 per cent tariff on nearly USD 28 billion worth of Canadian imports from 12:01 am ET.
The levies affect nearly 5.5 per cent of Canada's total exports shipped across the southern border, with targeted items ranging from hockey sticks to cement.
Carney said Ottawa would not accept any restrictions on its ability to independently execute trade deals around the globe.
He emphasised Ottawa's position as a sovereign global trade partner.
'The U.S. introduced at the last hours, in the last hours, efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals. You heard me say a moment ago what we've accomplished in the last year, 20 new deals, economic and security partnership, the prospect of doubling our market access because we believe in free trade. We're the partner of choice in many respects for countries around the world and the Americans wanted to restrict that,' Prime Minister Carney said.
'They had language that they wanted to restrict that. Unacceptable. But when it moves into restrictions and using Canada effectively as more leverage for America, that I mean clearly that's Canadians wouldn't accept that. We're a proud independent country. We've got the right values. We'll make our decisions about who we want to trade with and how and including on how we work with the United States,' he added.
He reiterated that any clause attempting to curb Canada's commercial flexibility remains a firm red line.
'Then there's a separate issue and I'll just stop with a sentence here which was language which suggested restrictions in terms of our ability to execute trade deals which would always be unacceptable to this government. Around the world that's expanding rapidly that will continue to expand because we're trusted, because we're reliable, because we have things like critical minerals, many other aspects that the world wants and so we're going to continue to pursue that and one thing that we certainly were not going to accept was any restriction in our ability to execute those deals,' PM Carney said.
Despite claims by US President Donald Trump that a mutual agreement remained achievable owing to his 'good relationship' with the Prime Minister, Ottawa confirmed it would retaliate against the new US trade barriers 'dollar for dollar'.
Taking to social media platform X, PM Carney wrote, 'Canada will match the U.S.' new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses. We take this step confident that it is in the best interests of Canada.'
The reciprocal measures announced by Ottawa will specifically focus on American dairy and steel exports, with the retaliatory duty structure scheduled to come into effect on September 8.

The diplomatic impasse comes after the White House accused Canada of 'discriminatory treatment' regarding imported US dairy, automobile, and alcohol products prior to imposing the new duties. (ANI)

sources.news_title: Canada-US Trade Rift Deepens as Carney Rejects ‘Bad Deal’ and Announces Retaliatory Tariffs
sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States after trade negotiations between the two longtime allies collapsed, escalating an already damaging economic dispute and raising fresh concerns about the future of North American trade relations.
Carney said Saturday that Canada had been prepared to reach a mutually beneficial agreement with Washington but ultimately rejected terms proposed by US President Donald Trump’s administration, describing them as economically damaging and unfair.
The breakdown came after Canadian and US negotiators spent much of the week in Washington attempting to resolve a series of disputes over tariffs and market access. With the talks failing, new US tariffs of 50 percent on a range of Canadian products came into force, affecting goods worth about US$20 billion, or roughly 5.5 percent of Canada’s exports to the United States.
The affected products include a wide range of Canadian goods, from hockey sticks and cement to other industrial and consumer products.
Speaking in Ottawa, Carney said Canada had entered the negotiations with the expectation that the two countries could reach an agreement.
“We believed earlier this week that we were moving towards a mutually beneficial agreement,” he said.
But, according to Carney, the US position changed during the final stages of the negotiations.
“In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal,” he said.
“In short, they asked too much and they offered too little.”
Carney said Canada would not accept the proposed conditions.
“We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked,” he said.
The Canadian prime minister went further, describing Washington’s tariff policy as a trade war.
“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said.
Canada’s response will include new tariffs targeting US steel and dairy industries. The measures are scheduled to take effect on September 8, with Carney saying further details will be announced next week.
The move marks another major escalation in the economic confrontation between the two countries, whose economies have traditionally been deeply integrated through decades of cross-border trade and investment.
Canada has been particularly vulnerable to US tariffs because of the scale of its economic dependence on the American market. Roughly 70 percent of Canadian exports are destined for the United States, making the relationship one of the most important pillars of Canada’s economy.
Carney acknowledged that dependence while arguing that the latest dispute had demonstrated the need for Canada to diversify its economic relationships.
“We’ve been under no illusions. We recognized from the start that America has changed,” Carney told reporters Saturday.
His comments reflect a broader shift in Canadian economic strategy since Trump returned to the White House and revived an aggressive approach to tariffs and trade negotiations.
For decades, Canada and the United States have operated one of the world’s most closely integrated bilateral trading relationships. Supply chains stretch across the border in sectors ranging from automobiles and energy to agriculture, manufacturing and construction.
The latest tariff confrontation threatens to disrupt those links further.
The Trump administration has presented the negotiations differently, arguing that Washington had offered Canada substantial tariff relief in return for concessions.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Friday that the United States had offered “significant tariff reductions” covering steel, aluminum, automobiles and lumber.
In return, Washington wanted Canada to make concessions on several issues that the White House considers barriers to US trade.
The White House has also accused Canada of discriminatory treatment of US alcohol, automobile and dairy products.
The tariffs were originally scheduled to take effect on Wednesday. Trump delayed their implementation by three days, saying that significant progress had been made during negotiations.
Trump has also expressed optimism about his relationship with Carney.
Speaking earlier, Trump said Washington “should be able to have a deal with Canada,” pointing to what he described as his good relationship with the Canadian prime minister.
Despite that public optimism, however, the talks ultimately failed to produce an agreement.
A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described the negotiations as candid but not acrimonious. The official said there were currently no additional meetings scheduled.
The absence of planned negotiations raises concerns that the dispute could persist unless both governments find a way to reopen discussions.
Canada has already experienced significant economic pressure from US tariffs on automobiles, steel and aluminum.
Canadian businesses have warned that tariffs are increasing production costs, disrupting supply chains and threatening jobs in industries heavily dependent on cross-border commerce.
The automotive sector is particularly exposed because vehicles and components frequently cross the US-Canada border multiple times during the manufacturing process.
Higher tariffs can therefore increase costs at several stages of production before a finished vehicle reaches consumers.
Steel and aluminum tariffs pose similar challenges because these materials are essential inputs for manufacturing, construction and transportation.
Canadian officials have argued that US tariffs ultimately hurt companies and consumers on both sides of the border by increasing costs and weakening the competitiveness of integrated North American industries.
The new Canadian measures against US steel and dairy products are intended to increase pressure on Washington while protecting Canada’s negotiating position.
Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus, a former US commerce official who now works with King & Spalding, said both countries would face pressure to find a way out of the escalating dispute.
“Both sides will face significant pressure in the coming days to find an off-ramp,” Majerus said.
That pressure could increase as businesses begin to experience the full impact of the new tariffs.
The latest confrontation also comes at a sensitive moment because Washington and Ottawa still face the much larger question of the future of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA.
The trade pact replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement and governs a huge portion of economic activity across North America.
Trump has already indicated that he does not want to simply extend the existing arrangement in its current form.
Any future negotiations over the agreement could therefore become more complicated because of the latest tariff dispute.
For Canada, securing predictable access to the US market is considered essential. For Washington, the trade relationship provides American industries with access to Canadian consumers, raw materials and integrated supply chains.
The challenge for both governments will be to prevent the tariff dispute from expanding into a broader breakdown of the North American trading system.
The economic conflict has also become intertwined with political tensions between Ottawa and Washington.
Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada could become the 51st US state, comments that have angered Canadian political leaders and strengthened nationalist sentiment in Canada.
Carney has responded by emphasizing Canadian sovereignty and the need to rethink the country’s economic dependence on its southern neighbor.
The deterioration in relations has been particularly notable because Canada and the United States have historically been among the world’s closest political, military and economic partners.
The two countries cooperate extensively on defense and border security and share a vast and highly integrated economic relationship.
But Trump’s tariff policies have increasingly challenged the assumption that the relationship will remain stable simply because of its long history.
Carney’s comments at the World Economic Forum in Davos earlier this year also appeared to irritate Trump.
In a widely discussed January speech, Carney warned that the international economic order was experiencing a “rupture,” signaling that Canada could no longer assume that longstanding alliances and economic arrangements would continue unchanged.
Since then, the Canadian prime minister has repeatedly argued that his country must reduce its dependence on the US economy.
The latest breakdown in negotiations appears to have reinforced that position.
Carney’s government now faces the difficult task of balancing retaliation against the United States with the need to protect Canadian businesses from further disruption.
Retaliatory tariffs may increase political and economic pressure on Washington, but they can also raise costs for Canadian companies and consumers if the dispute continues.
At the same time, simply accepting US demands could expose Canada to further economic pressure and weaken Ottawa’s negotiating position in future trade discussions.
The government therefore faces a delicate calculation: how far to retaliate while keeping open the possibility of renewed negotiations.
For Canada, the dispute has also accelerated a broader debate about economic diversification.
Reducing reliance on the United States would require Canada to expand trade with Europe, Asia and other international markets while improving domestic infrastructure and supply chains.
Such a shift would not happen quickly. The geographic proximity of the United States, combined with decades of integrated production networks, makes the American market uniquely important to Canada.
Nevertheless, Carney’s government increasingly sees diversification as a strategic necessity rather than simply an economic preference.
The collapse of the latest negotiations underscores the scale of that challenge.
What began as a dispute over tariffs has now evolved into a broader confrontation over the rules governing one of the world’s most integrated bilateral economic relationships.
With Canadian retaliation scheduled for September 8 and no further US-Canada meetings currently planned, pressure will mount on both governments to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
For Carney, however, the message from Ottawa is clear: Canada is no longer prepared to accept what it considers an unequal trade arrangement simply to preserve the traditional status quo.

Canadian PM vows ‘dollar-for-dollar’ tariffs against US as trade talks collapse

The prime minister said the counter-tariffs will cover a wide range of sectors, including dairy, steel, appliances, pulp and paper, and electronics.
The United States and Canada failed to reach a trade deal on Friday, and the United States imposed a 50 per cent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods on Saturday which took effect just after midnight (0400 GMT), reports Xinhua news agency.
Explaining why negotiations broke down at the last minute, Carney said that while both sides were close to a mutually beneficial agreement earlier this week, the US side introduced last-minute changes that were “unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
The US side’s repeated disregard for existing free trade agreements such as the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) sends a bad signal to international businesses and is “certainly not good news” for renewing the agreement in the future, Carney warned.
The rift comes as the United States, Mexico and Canada are trying to renew the CUSMA, a trade agreement that Trump negotiated in his first term and once praised as a triumph.
The United States has begun formal talks with Mexico to revamp the agreement, but talks with Canada have not yet begun.
The CUSMA is a trilateral trade pact that replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement when it took effect on July 1, 2020. On July 1, 2026, the United States officially declined to renew the agreement for another 16-year term, triggering an annual review process until the pact expires in 2036.
When asked why Canada was entering a trade dispute, the prime minister stated flatly: “Because we were attacked.”
Carney reiterated his confidence in Canada’s economic resilience, pointing out that Canada is creating jobs at four times the rate of the United States, with foreign direct investment reaching a 20-year high.
“Canada is becoming stronger and less dependent on America,” he said.

sources.news_title: TARIFF WAR: Canada Strikes Back – Retaliatory US Tariffs Set for Sept. 8
sources.text:
Canada announced Saturday that it will impose retaliatory tariffs against the United States beginning Sept. 8, escalating a rapidly widening trade confrontation after President Donald Trump’s 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion in Canadian goods took effect and last-minute negotiations between the longtime allies collapsed.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa will release specifics of the retaliatory package shortly, with the new duties targeting a broad range of American products.
“in the coming days, we will release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labor Day.”
Canada plans to retaliate on a dollar-for-dollar basis, with steel, dairy products, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics among the sectors expected to be targeted.
Carney revealed that during negotiations, Canada had offered to eliminate its remaining retaliatory tariffs on American steel, aluminum and automobiles if Washington substantially reduced its own tariffs. Ottawa was also prepared to encourage Canadian provinces to resume sales of US alcohol.
The prime minister said the final terms sought by Washington were ultimately unacceptable.
“They asked too much and offered too little.”
The deepening dispute is also raising new questions about the future of the broader North American trade framework linking the United States, Canada and Mexico, an agreement upon which major industries in all three countries heavily depend.
Canada had entered the negotiations seeking tariff relief for several key industries, including steel, aluminum, automobiles and lumber.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer placed responsibility for the failed negotiations on Ottawa, arguing that Canadian officials retreated from commitments made earlier in the week.
“Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week. Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk-backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” Greer said in a statement read to reporters shortly before midnight.
Carney offered a sharply different account of why negotiations failed, accusing the Trump administration of changing its demands as the deadline approached.
“last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
The Canadian leader said his government will also unveil additional measures in the coming days aimed at assisting Canadian businesses and workers affected by the expanding trade battle.
Greer characterized Washington’s proposal as “forward-looking” and said it offered “a historic economic and national security partnership.”
For now, there are no additional negotiations scheduled between the two governments.
The collapse represented a dramatic turnaround from the optimism expressed only two days earlier, when officials on both sides indicated that Washington and Ottawa appeared to be moving toward an agreement.
Carney said Canada had always sought the strongest possible arrangement for the country, “never a deal at any price or on any deadline.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford threw his support behind Carney’s decision to retaliate. Ford said the prime minister has his “full support” for a response conducted “tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar” and insisted that “everything needs to be on the table.”
The economic stakes are enormous. The United States and Canada exchanged approximately $880 billion in goods and services last year, making their bilateral commercial relationship one of the largest in the world.
Trump’s tariffs had initially been scheduled to take effect at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday. The president extended the deadline by three days as negotiations intensified, but officials ultimately failed to reach an agreement before the new deadline expired.
Trade disputes between Washington and Ottawa are hardly new. The neighboring countries have sparred for decades over issues ranging from Canadian softwood lumber to American access to Canada’s tightly controlled dairy market.
Despite those recurring disagreements, the two countries traditionally maintained an unusually close economic, military and diplomatic relationship. Canadian troops fought alongside American forces in Afghanistan following the Sept. 11 attacks, while the 5,525-mile US-Canada border has remained undefended. Nearly 330,000 people and approximately $2 billion in goods cross the border every day, while roughly 800,000 Canadians reside in the United States.
Trump’s treatment of Canada has represented a significant break from that traditionally cooperative relationship. The president has used tariffs as part of his effort to shift manufacturing back to the United States and has repeatedly generated controversy in Canada by suggesting that the country could become America’s 51st state.
Carney said his government has come to recognize that “America has changed” and that Canada and the United States would “not return to our old relationship.”
Anti-American sentiment has also grown among some Canadians. A petition calling for the expulsion of US Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, a Trump ally, has attracted nearly 248,000 signatures since July 21. Organizers have accused Hoekstra of having “normalized” Trump’s comments about annexing Canada, among other complaints.
Both governments nevertheless faced significant incentives to avoid an escalating tariff war.
Almost 72% of Canadian goods exports went to the United States last year, making access to the American market critical to Canada’s economy. At the same time, the Trump administration faces the possibility that additional tariffs — which are paid initially by American importers and can ultimately be passed on to consumers — could increase prices ahead of November’s midterm elections, when the cost of living remains a major concern for voters.
“Canada likely wanted further sector-specific relief than the U.S. was willing to offer, or Canada’s concessions did not go far enough,” said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former U.S. trade official. “Either way, I think both sides will be under immense pressure in the coming days to still find an off-ramp. But if Canada has agreed to also impose tariffs, the off-ramp may be even harder to find.”
Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, described the new tariffs as “a body blow to North American competitiveness” and warned that the escalating dispute could increase costs for American consumers while hurting Canadian customers, investment and small businesses.

Mark Carney Needs a Wartime Counterpropaganda Machine
August 22, 2026
If there were any doubt about our current relationship with the United States after the collapse of trade talks on Friday night, Prime Minister Mark Carney, in his press conference on Saturday, provided Canadians with all the clarity necessary: we were attacked so, yes, this is a trade war.
This is not, strictly speaking, a war between Canadians and Americans. It is a war on Canadian economic integrity and sovereignty by a rogue regime in Washington already causing so much unprecedented political, geopolitical, military, institutional and reputational damage to America that the inventory of self-inflicted catastrophes is too long to list here.
This creates a communications challenge that takes the communications challenge inherent in any wartime strategy to a whole new level.
As in any war where one aggressor nation attempts to prey on another, the casus belli for an attack must be established by the former.
Donald Trump has an intuitive, compulsive need to declare his intentions and his reasons for his actions via social media, of course, even if those intentions and reasons can change daily – or hourly.
However, the work of threading together a more coherent narrative, one no less aggressive or pernicious, is carried out by his team of enablers in synch. Now more than ever, it is vital, given our proximity to America and its cultural influence on this country, that there is a strong correction of Trumpian propaganda coming from Ottawa.
Carney’s Forward Guidance videos, billed as semi-regular updates or fireside chats, have suddenly become much more pertinent. The first two put to bed any question about the Prime Minister’s ability to be both an effective and engaging communicator.
Those talents now have to be martialed for a new context and the battle ahead; Carney will need to double down on difference, to highlight the fact that this isn’t just an economic war, but a war on the very truth of who we are and what Canada is.
Historical amnesia — or simply historical ignorance — can be so easily weaponized, as this new era of Trumpism has handily proven.
If we are indeed at war, it will require an air war as well as a ground war to defend us from a different kind of attack: the one on our sovereignty.
We have experienced aggressive trade tactics from Trump’s America before, but we’re facing a different enemy in this conflict. Trump 1.0 framed the invocation of the Section 232 tariffs as a corrective measure to reinvigorate the domestic production of materials, slated for defense purposes, made from steel, aluminum and copper.
However, these measures were also framed as creating a revival of heartland America, shining up the Rust Belt so that it glowed with all the promise of salvation for communities left behind as the American economy evolved over the previous four decades.
The rationale for the latest round of Section 338 tariffs, coming from Trump 2.0, is markedly different. It has given us something that most Ukrainians lived through, prior to 2022: the insidious discrediting, by Russia, of any claim to sovereignty their nation could claim. We’re now seeing the same page of that playbook at work.
Trump’s high-ranking officials have re-framed our bilateral relationship as if they are Russia and we are Ukraine. They view Canada as naturally, or inevitably, subservient to the economic power of the US.
When they attempt to flatter, they describe this subservience as ultimately good for us. We’re so much like them, really. We want the same products, consume the same entertainment. Why should we fixate on the narcissism of small differences?
This is an attempt to arrest our defenses, of course. It characterizes any response to aggression as the acting out, or misbehaviour, of a vassal state. It positions our sense of sovereignty as a delusion, a state of denial, that we’ve somehow, perhaps subconsciously misread or misconceived our own historic sense of national identity.
There will quite likely be more of this rhetoric from Washington in the days ahead. We’re not the target audience for this messaging, of course, though it will appeal to a certain constituency on this side of the border, too.
This is why the Prime Minister needs an air-war strategy.
Historical amnesia — or simply historical ignorance — can be so easily weaponized, as this new era of Trumpism has handily proven.
A concerted, serialized effort to explain why particular counter-tariffs will be selected, how we’re building Canada, and how this is fundamental to our legacy and the country’s promise, will help inoculate us from disinformation designed to attack our sovereignty.
And if by chance some Americans are also inoculated in the process, so much the better.
Policy Contributing Writer John Delacourt is Senior Vice President of Counsel Public Affairs in Ottawa and a veteran Liberal strategist. He is the author of several novels, including The Innocent Canadian.

By Enyichukwu Enemanna
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday announced that he would slap retaliatory tariffs on the United States after walking away from a “bad deal” on trade, deepening the rift between the longtime allies.
Negotiations between the neighbouring countries broke down on Friday in Washington, allowing new 50-percent US tariffs impacting some $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States, to come into force.
US President Donald Trump had said Washington “should be able to have a deal with Canada,” citing his “good relationship” with Carney.
But on Saturday, the Canadian Prime Minister said Trump had set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable.
“We believed earlier this week that we were moving towards a mutually beneficial agreement,” Carney said in the Canadian capital Ottawa.
“In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal. In short, they asked too much and they offered too little,” he said.
“We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked,” Carney said, accusing Trump of launching a trade “war.”
“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney said.
New Canadian tariffs will notably target the US steel and dairy industries, and take effect on September 8. Carney said further details would come next week.
On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington had offered “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber” in exchange for concessions from Canada.
A senior US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, characterized the talks as candid and not acrimonious, but said there were no further scheduled meetings.
Canada has been seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.
Canadian negotiators had been camped out in Washington this week to firm up a deal that aimed to address various flashpoints.
The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.

sources.news_title: US and Canada fall deeper into trade war as talks collapse
sources.text:
Negotiations between the United States and Canada collapsed late Friday, August 21, 2026, in Washington, leading the U.S. to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods starting Saturday. The tariffs, announced by President Donald Trump in July and delayed after a tentative deal, were implemented after talks failed to resolve disputes over alleged discriminatory treatment of U.S. products, officials said.
The tariffs took effect at 12:01 a.m. Saturday, August 22, 2026, and apply to about $20 billion in Canadian exports, covering a broad range of goods including automobiles, heavy trucks, dairy products, alcohol, cement, essential oils, honey, wine, and hockey sticks, according to officials at the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR). Canadian government sources estimated the affected exports at approximately 28 billion Canadian dollars (about €17 billion), or nearly 5% of Canada’s annual exports to the U.S.
The 50% duty rate represents a significant escalation from previous rounds of tariffs in the ongoing 2025–2026 trade conflict between the two countries.
The collapse of negotiations followed intensive talks in Washington throughout the week of August 18, with a tentative deal reached on August 18–19 that prompted President Donald Trump to announce a three-day pause on the tariffs. The pause was intended to allow time for finalizing documents, setting a new deadline of August 22. However, by late Friday, August 21, USTR officials said Canada refused to finalize the agreement under terms previously agreed upon, citing new demands from the Canadian side, including requests for lower tariffs on heavy trucks. These last-minute Canadian “new asks” were publicly blamed by Trump and senior U.S. officials for derailing the negotiations.
Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, countered that internal disagreements within the Trump administration over control of key deal elements contributed to the breakdown. Ottawa emphasized a firmness strategy, refusing provisions it considered harmful and accusing the U.S. of using the tariff deadline as leverage rather than seeking genuine compromise, according to Canadian government statements. Canadian officials also disputed the U.S. characterization that the tariffs were retaliation for discriminatory Canadian treatment of U.S. cars, alcohol, and dairy products.
In response to the U.S. tariffs, the Canadian government pledged to impose retaliatory tariffs “dollar for dollar,” with Carney announcing that Canadian countermeasures would take effect on September 8, 2026. While specific product lists had not been fully detailed publicly as of August 22, Canadian officials indicated a broad array of U.S. consumer and industrial goods would be targeted. This symmetrical retaliation marks a reversal of earlier Canadian tariff adjustments, which had dropped many retaliatory tariffs overlapping with exemptions under the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) to facilitate negotiations.
The new tariffs risk disrupting deeply integrated North American supply chains, with business groups warning that more than $1 trillion in annual trade could be affected. The automotive sector is a particular area of concern, as tariffs on vehicles and heavy trucks threaten cross-border production lines and jobs on both sides of the border. Trade organizations have cautioned that the measures could put up to 13 million American jobs linked to trade under USMCA at risk. Canadian businesses, especially in already struggling industries, anticipate job losses and higher costs due to both the U.S. tariffs and anticipated Canadian retaliation, according to industry sources.
Negotiations had appeared to be progressing well as recently as August 13, with a Canadian government source stating that talks were advancing and that Washington also wanted a deal before the tariff deadline. However, over the following week, core issues such as autos, agriculture, and dispute-settlement rules remained unresolved. The three-day pause announced on August 18 provided a brief window for finalizing the deal, but last-minute U.S. demands and Canadian counterproposals undermined the fragile agreement, leading to the collapse by late August 21. Reports following the tariff imposition indicated no further talks were planned in the immediate aftermath.
The escalation into a renewed trade war between the United States and Canada adds a new front to the broader 2025–2026 U.S. trade conflict involving Mexico and other partners. Analysts and media have noted that the expanded tariffs exceed previous rounds in both rate and product coverage, raising prices for consumers in both countries through increased costs in sectors such as autos, food, construction materials, and consumer goods. Mexico, deeply integrated into North American supply chains, is also seen as potentially affected by the intensifying U.S.–Canada dispute.
The trade war context remains politically charged, with ongoing strategic competition and “continuous negotiation” expected despite the current breakdown. The failure to reach an agreement and the imposition of tariffs mark a significant moment in the bilateral trade relationship, with economic and political ramifications likely to unfold in the coming months.

For Canadian and US businesses, the next stage will depend on whether the two governments return to negotiations or allow the tariff dispute to continue.
For now, Canada has set September 8 as the date when its retaliatory measures will begin.

sources.news_title: Canada Counter-Tariffs Set for Sept. 8 Following U.S. Trade Breakdown
Canada Announces Retaliatory Tariffs on US Goods
sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced retaliatory tariffs on United States (US) goods after rejecting what he called an unfair trade offer from President Donald Trump.
The announcement came on Saturday after trade talks between Canada and the United States broke down in Washington on Friday.
The collapse of the talks has allowed new 50 percent US tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods to take effect.
The affected products include hockey sticks, cement and other goods, representing about 5.5 percent of Canada’s exports to the United States.
Carney said Washington had demanded too much while offering too little during the negotiations.
“We cannot accept what they’ve offered, and we will not give what they’ve asked,” he said, accusing Trump of starting a trade “war.”
“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” Carney added.
Canada’s new tariffs will target US steel and dairy products and take effect on September 8.
Carney said further details would be announced next week.
Trump had earlier said the two countries should be able to reach an agreement, pointing to his “good relationship” with Carney.
However, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington had offered significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber in exchange for concessions from Canada.
A senior US official said the negotiations were direct but not hostile, adding that no further meetings had been scheduled.
Canada has been seeking relief from US tariffs on automobiles, steel and aluminium, which Ottawa says have hurt its economy, caused job losses and strained relations between the two countries.
The latest dispute comes as both countries prepare to renegotiate the North American trade agreement, USMCA.
Relations have also been strained by Trump’s repeated comments about making Canada the 51st US state.
Carney said Canada must reduce its dependence on the United States, which currently accounts for about 70 percent of Canadian exports.
“We’ve been under no illusions. We recognized from the start that America has changed,” Carney told reporters on Saturday.
Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus said both countries would face “significant pressure” to find a way out of the dispute.

sources.news_title: Canada's PM Carney announces retaliatory measures against US effective September 8
sources.text:
Via pm.gc.ca
Canada’s PM Carney announces retaliatory measures against US effective September 8
Canada suspends trade negotiations and prepares a multi-billion dollar support package after the US slapped 50% tariffs on Canadian exports
Canada and the United States are in the middle of their ugliest trade fight in recent memory, and it just got worse. Prime Minister Mark Carney has suspended trade negotiations with Washington and announced a package of retaliatory measures set to take effect on September 8.
The trigger: a 50% US tariff on roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian exports that went into effect around August 21. Carney described the last-minute demands from US negotiators as unfair, and rather than continuing to talk, Canada walked away from the table.
What Canada is actually doing
The September 8 package is a two-pronged response. On the offensive side, Canada plans to impose equivalent tariffs on US goods, matching the pain dollar for dollar. On the defensive side, Ottawa is rolling out targeted support for industries caught in the crossfire.
That support includes a $5 billion fund aimed at businesses directly impacted by the tariffs. Sectors like dairy, alcohol, and automotive are expected to be the primary beneficiaries, given their heavy exposure to cross-border trade.
Atlantic Canada is set to receive $80 million in dedicated regional funding.
Canada actually rolled back some of its existing 25% retaliatory tariffs on US goods effective September 1, a move that looked like an olive branch at the time. One week later, the new measures kick in.
How negotiations fell apart
Carney placed the blame squarely on Washington’s negotiating posture. According to the Prime Minister, the US introduced demands at the last minute that were fundamentally unacceptable. Rather than capitulate, Canada chose confrontation.
US-Canada trade relations have been marked by periodic flare-ups for years, with tariffs on steel and aluminum serving as recurring friction points.
Market implications and what to watch
For investors, the immediate concern is volatility in sectors with heavy cross-border exposure. Canadian dairy producers, automakers, and alcohol exporters face direct margin pressure from the US tariffs. Their American counterparts selling into Canada will feel the same squeeze once retaliatory duties land on September 8.
Automotive supply chains are particularly vulnerable. Parts cross the US-Canada border multiple times during assembly, and each crossing now potentially triggers tariff costs.
